question: Article 13 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union1 stipulates that, in formulating and implementing the EU’s agriculture policy, the EU should pay full regard to animal welfare. However, there appears to be no general EU legislation that ensures the welfare of wild animals in situations where protection is both needed and feasible.

There are growing welfare challenges for wild animals that are injured or killed during the harvest of crops. Similarly, road traffic poses a major threat to wildlife, with extensive roadkills occurring due to insufficient fencing or other preventive measures along major roads. Technical and practical solutions already exist which could significantly reduce unnecessary suffering and mortality among wild animals.
In the light of this: 1.

Does the Commission agree that the EU should also seek to ‘pay full regard to the welfare requirements’ of wild animals, and that there is currently no comprehensive legislation ensuring the practical application of these welfare considerations for wild animals, comparable to that which exists for kept animals?

Does the Commission consider it appropriate to review current EU legislation to assess the need for supplementary measures or new legal instruments that could, among other things, promote the development and application of technical solutions to better safeguard the welfare of wild animals2?

OJ C 326, 26.10.2012, pp. 47–390, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/treaty/tfeu_2012/oj. A Danish report from Aarhus University (2006) cites studies estimating that around 15 % of leverets were killed by harvesting machinery during the time covered by the studies, rising to up to 45 % in certain crop types.

A subsequent Danish study (2017) estimated that approximately 20 000 roe deer fawns are killed annually in Denmark by harvesting machinery. There is growing interest across several Member States in developing technologies such as drones capable of detecting a significant proportion of fawns prior to mowing; however, their use remains limited both nationally and across the EU.
answer: Article 13 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) requires the EU and its Member States to pay full regard to animal welfare requirements when formulating and implementing the EU’s agriculture, fisheries, transport, internal market, research and technological development and space policies. This is an integration principle that must inform EU policy and legislation.

As such, EU legislation considers wild animal welfare requirements where these appear most relevant, through legislation on humane trapping standards (1), leghold-traps (2) and seal products (3), and through the Invasive Alien Species Regulation (4) and the Wildlife Trade Regulation (5).

Furthermore, in the frame of its support for the implementation of the Birds (6) and Habitats Directives (7) the Commission also promotes the exchange of best practises and new technologies to avoid accidental injury or killing of protected species.
On that basis, the Commission considers that sufficient steps have been taken in relation to those EU policy-related activities which are most relevant to the welfare of wild animals.
